prompt: A model is given a very long document with one crucial instruction far back in it, and the reply ignores the instruction. Which `toylm` behaviour is the same failure on a smaller scale?

choices.text: `the cat sat on the` ended on the chair, because `sat` was out of its two-word window
choices.why: Right. Text outside the model's view has no say in what comes next, whether the window is two words or a very long one.

choices.text: `the coffee is` gave `hot` three times in five draws
choices.why: That is weighted drawing, which happens with the whole prompt in view.

choices.text: `sweet` got no score at all after `coffee is`
choices.why: That is a pair never seen in the training file, not text the model failed to see in the prompt.

choices.text: `the café opens at` gave `seven` at 75%
choices.why: That is the model working with its whole context in view and scoring what followed it.

prompt: `toylm next "the coffee is"` gave `bitter` 3.7%. Drawing in proportion to the scores, about once in how many draws does `bitter` come out? Answer to the nearest whole number.
Somebody edits `corpus.txt` so that `cold` follows `coffee is` far more than `hot` does, and rebuilds `toylm`. What changes in `toylm next "the coffee is"`?

choices.text: Nothing, because the program has learnt that coffee is served hot
choices.why: It has learnt nothing about coffee; it has counts of which word followed which pair.

choices.text: `hot` keeps the top score and `cold` appears as a new second line
choices.why: The order comes straight from the counts, so the word counted most is the one on top.

choices.text: `cold` gets the top score, since the scores are the new counts
choices.why: Right. Nothing about coffee is known apart from the counts, so new counts are new scores.

choices.text: The output is refused, because the new file contradicts a fact
choices.why: There is no store of facts to contradict, only the counts in its file.

prompt: In the twenty-run test, how many more replies containing `seven` did `v3` get than `v1`?
Match each part of a prompt to what goes wrong when it is missing.

pairs.right: The model guesses the task
The model fills the gap with what is typical
There is nothing to be right about
A correct reply that cannot be used where it is going

right_distractors: The reply is too long to read

prompt: To save money, an application sends the model only the newest user message on each turn. What will users notice?

choices.text: The assistant forgets everything said earlier in the conversation
choices.why: Right. The model has no memory between requests; the earlier turns reach it only because the application sends them again.

choices.text: Nothing, because the model remembers the earlier turns of the session
choices.why: It keeps nothing between requests. What looks like memory is the whole conversation, sent again every time.

choices.text: Replies get slower, since the model has to look up the earlier turns itself
choices.why: There is nowhere for it to look them up. What is not in the request does not exist for the model.

choices.text: The system message is dropped, but the rest of the conversation is kept
choices.why: The earlier user and assistant turns are exactly what was cut, and they are not kept anywhere else.

prompt: A prompt that passed its tests last month now fails them, and five edits were made since. Which habit lets you find the edit that caused it?

choices.text: A stated goal
choices.why: The goal says what a good reply is. It does not tell you which of five edits broke it.

choices.text: Measuring over many runs
choices.why: Measuring says that it fails now. Finding which edit did it needs the old versions.

choices.text: Test cases
choices.why: The tests are how you noticed. Without the earlier versions you cannot run them against each edit.

choices.text: Versioning
choices.why: Right. Every version kept and named is what lets a regression be traced to the change that caused it.

prompt: Counted with `cl100k_base`, how many more tokens is `hours.pt.txt` than `hours.en.txt`?
A request pastes a twenty-page contract into the prompt and asks for a one-line answer. Which side of the bill does lesson 3 expect to dominate?

choices.text: The output, since output tokens always cost several times more
choices.why: They cost more each. With a one-line reply and a long document, there are too few of them to dominate.

choices.text: Neither, since a request is priced as a whole and not by its parts
choices.why: Providers bill input and output per token, separately.

choices.text: The input, since the contract is far more tokens than the reply
choices.why: Right. Output tokens cost more each, and here there are so few of them that the input outweighs them.

choices.text: The output, since the model has to read the contract while writing
choices.why: Reading the contract is input, processed in one pass and billed as input.

prompt: Your provider does not publish its tokenizer. You count your prompts with `tok`, using `o200k_base`. How should you treat those counts?

choices.text: As exact, since every modern model uses `o200k_base`
choices.why: Other providers use tokenizers of their own. At the time of writing, `o200k_base` is OpenAI's.

choices.text: As estimates: get the real count from the provider
choices.why: Right. A count from one tokenizer is an estimate for any other; the provider counts for you through its API.

choices.text: As useless, since counts from two tokenizers share nothing
choices.why: They are close enough to estimate with, as the handbook counts in lesson 12 showed. They are not exact.

choices.text: As an upper bound, since bigger vocabularies always use fewer tokens
choices.why: Fewer for some texts, not a guarantee for every text and every other tokenizer.

prompt: `tok fit` keeps the 53-token system prompt, then turns from the newest back until the next one would not fit. The newest three turns of `chat.json` are 14, 21 and 10 tokens. With `-b 90`, how many turns would it keep?
An application writes a summary note before dropping old turns, and the note leaves out Bruno's nut allergy. What does lesson 4 say about that?

choices.text: Nothing can be done, since notes are always incomplete
choices.why: Lesson 4 gives the remedy: a summarising prompt that names what must survive.

choices.text: Notes should be dropped, since truncation loses less
choices.why: Truncation lost the allergy outright at a budget of 120. A note that names what to keep saved it.

choices.text: The note should go in a user turn, where it is read more closely
choices.why: User turns are the part that gets cut. The note travels in the part that is never cut.

choices.text: The summarising prompt has to say what must survive
choices.why: Right. A summary can lose the one detail that mattered as easily as truncation, so the prompt names what to keep: name, allergies, preferences, promises.

prompt: Match each part of a request to what makes it grow in the context window.

pairs.right: Somebody adds a rule
The conversation goes on
A document or a tool result is included
The model writes

right_distractors: The model learns from the chat

prompt: After `the soup of the day is`, `toylm` scored tomato 50%, lentil 25% and pumpkin 25%. Drawing in proportion to the scores, in what percentage of draws is the answer something other than tomato?
A customer asks the café's assistant: "Why did you stop selling oat milk?" The café still sells it. Which shape from lesson 5's table is the risk?

choices.text: A citation with the right shape that does not exist
choices.why: That is the risk when you ask for a source. Nobody asked for one here.

choices.text: A reply that accepts the false premise and explains it
choices.why: Right. Text that answers a question is likelier than text that disputes it, so a reason for a change that never happened is the likely reply.

choices.text: The old value of a fact that has changed, in the present tense
choices.why: Nothing changed: the premise is false, not out of date.

choices.text: A plausible fact about something similar to a rare one
choices.why: Oat milk at a café is not rare. The trap is in the question's assumption.

prompt: After adding "if the sources do not contain the answer, say that the handbook does not say", a team's score drops: their test counts only the questions that got an answer. What does lesson 5 say?

choices.text: The test rewards the behaviour the line removes; count the honest refusal as a success
choices.why: Right. A short "the handbook does not say" is a success, and a test that counts only answers punishes it.

choices.text: The line made the assistant worse, and should come out
choices.why: It made an honest reply likely. The test is what needs changing.

choices.text: Lower the temperature, so the assistant answers more of the questions
choices.why: Temperature is not a control for truth, and answering more is not the goal here.

choices.text: Add "Do not make things up" too, so the score recovers
choices.why: That line helps very little, since the model does not know which likely answers are invented.

prompt: `agent runs/order.txt` calls `today` on step 1, the calculator on step 2 and answers on step 3. Run with `--max-steps 2`, how many tool calls happen before it stops?
A calculator tool is described to the model with the single word "Arithmetic", and the model keeps sending `sqrt(2)`, which the tool rejects. What does lesson 6 point to?

choices.text: Give the model a larger window, so it remembers the earlier errors
choices.why: The errors are already in front of it. What is missing is the sentence saying what the tool accepts.

choices.text: Raise the step limit, so the model finds the right form by trying
choices.why: Every extra turn costs tokens, and trial and error is what a clear description saves.

choices.text: Nothing: the model chose the call, so the fault lies with the model
choices.why: The model decides from that one sentence. A vague sentence is the developer's to fix.

choices.text: Rewrite the description to say which operations the tool takes
choices.why: Right. The description is a prompt too: "numbers and + - * /" tells the model what to send.

prompt: Match each kind of line in `agent`'s output to where it came from.

pairs.right: The model's turns, live or played back from a file
A real tool that ran
The loop, when a limit or the turns ran out

right_distractors: The customer who asked the question

prompt: An assistant drafts replies to the café's incoming e-mail, and a person sends each draft. Which set of tools follows lesson 7's least privilege?

choices.text: Read, draft and send, with a prompt line saying never to send
choices.why: A prompt line is not a control. If the task does not need sending, it does not get it.

choices.text: Inbox access and a place for unsent text, with no sending tool
choices.why: Right. The task drafts; sending is a person's job, so an injected e-mail has nothing to send with.

choices.text: Every mail tool, so the assistant is never stuck mid-task
choices.why: Every extra tool is something an injection can try to use.

choices.text: No tools, with the e-mails pasted in by hand each time
choices.why: That removes the job the assistant was built for. The aim is the tools the task needs, and no more.

prompt: Which of these still hold after the model has been fooled by an injection? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A call held until a person confirms it
choices.why: Yes. The person looks at the action itself, which the injection cannot disguise.

choices.text: A program that blocks e-mail to addresses outside the company
choices.why: Yes. It inspects the call before it is used.

choices.text: A system prompt line saying to ignore instructions in documents
choices.why: It competes with the injected text inside the same window, and the model has just lost that contest.

choices.text: A tool left off the task's allow-list
choices.why: Yes. The program refuses it whatever the model was persuaded of.

prompt: An assistant has no tools at all: it reads web pages a user pastes in and replies. Which aims of an injection remain open to a page's author?

choices.text: Misleading the reply, and leaking what is in the context into it
choices.why: Right. Acting needs a tool, and there is none; the reply itself is still a way out for a lie or a leak.

choices.text: None, since an assistant without tools cannot be injected
choices.why: Injection needs only text the model reads. The reply can still be steered.

choices.text: Acting, since the reply can send an e-mail on its own
choices.why: A reply is text. Without a tool, nothing in the conversation sends anything.

choices.text: Only leaking, since a reply cannot be made to say anything false
choices.why: Changing what the reply says is the third aim, and it needs nothing but the reply.

prompt: Using lesson 8's arithmetic, how many gigabytes do the weights of a 34B model take at 4 bits?
A laptop has 16 GB of memory, which also holds the operating system and the programs open on it. Which model's weights fit with room to spare?

choices.text: A 7B model at 16 bits, which is 14 GB
choices.why: It does not fit with room to spare: the operating system and the rest need memory too.

choices.text: A 70B model at 4 bits
choices.why: That is 35 GB even at 4 bits: a workstation or a server.

choices.text: A 7B model at 4 bits
choices.why: Right. 3.5 GB leaves plenty of room, including for the working memory a long context needs.

choices.text: A 7B model at full precision, 32 bits
choices.why: At 4 bytes a weight that is 28 GB, almost twice what the laptop has.

prompt: Storing each weight in fewer bits, rounded to a coarser set of values, is called ___.
A colleague says: "I set the model's parameters to temperature 0.2 and 300 tokens." What does lesson 8 say is mixed up?

choices.text: Nothing; parameters and settings are two words for one thing
choices.why: That is the borrowed word lesson 8 corrects. A model's parameters are what it learnt, and they do not change per request.

choices.text: Those are request settings; the parameters are the learnt weights
choices.why: Right. The model is its learnt numbers. Temperature and the token limit are things you pass with a request, lessons 13 to 17.

choices.text: Temperature is a weight, but the token limit is a setting
choices.why: Neither is a weight. Both are sent with the request and leave the weights untouched.

choices.text: The parameters are the sentences the model stored during its training
choices.why: The model stores no sentences. Its parameters are numbers, and what it read is spread across all of them.

prompt: At the illustrative prices, 10,000 requests cost 4.33 with `few-shot.txt` and 0.53 with `short.txt`. How much is saved over one million requests, in the same units?
Which costs of fine-tuning are not on the per-token bill? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Collecting and labelling hundreds of examples
choices.why: Yes, and it is usually the largest: people's time, checking each answer.

choices.text: Training runs, since the first is rarely the last
choices.why: Yes. Each run is billed, and the data is adjusted and trained again.

choices.text: An evaluation set held back from training
choices.why: Yes. Without it you cannot tell a good run from a bad one.

choices.text: The input tokens of each short request
choices.why: Those are exactly what the per-token bill counts.

prompt: A model was fine-tuned on the café's old opening hours, then trained again on the new ones. By lesson 9, what is still true?

choices.text: The second run overwrote the old hours, so only the new ones remain
choices.why: Training nudges weights; it does not replace a record. The old hours stay in there with no way to remove them.

choices.text: Nothing is left of the old hours once the new model is served
choices.why: The new model started from the old weights, and the old hours are part of them.

choices.text: The model now refuses questions about the hours, since it saw two answers
choices.why: It does not detect a conflict. It produces whichever continuation is likely, which may be either.

choices.text: The old hours are still spread through the weights, with no way to remove them
choices.why: Right. There is no way to delete a fact from billions of numbers, and the model produces likely text rather than stored records.

prompt: Replies come back in the wrong tone, and nobody has yet tried rewriting the prompt. The team proposes fine-tuning. What does lesson 9's ladder say?

choices.text: Fine-tune, since tone is a habit and habits are what training is good at
choices.why: Tone is a habit, and that makes fine-tuning possible later. The ladder climbs a rung only after the one below was tried and measured.

choices.text: Add retrieval, so the model can read the support team's earlier replies
choices.why: Retrieval is for knowledge the model lacks. A wrong tone is not a missing fact.

choices.text: Write a clearer prompt first, then add examples
choices.why: Right. Format and tone are the first two rungs, and fine-tuning is for a behaviour that already works with a long prompt.

choices.text: Collect labelled examples first, then decide between a prompt and training
choices.why: Labelling is the dearest part of fine-tuning, done before a minute was spent on the cheapest rung.

prompt: Which of these are machine learning, in lesson 10's sense? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A route planner following rules a programmer wrote
choices.why: AI in the field's sense, not machine learning, since nothing was learnt from examples.

choices.text: A spam filter trained on messages people marked as spam
choices.why: Yes: its behaviour was learnt from examples.

choices.text: `toylm`, counting which word followed each pair
choices.why: Yes. Nobody wrote the rule that `hot` follows `coffee is`; it was counted from the corpus.

choices.text: A chess program whose rules and scoring were written by hand
choices.why: It is AI, and it learnt nothing: every rule was written.

prompt: A benchmark's answers turn out to be `yes` for every question. Which of lesson 10's five questions catches that problem?

choices.text: What exactly was measured?
choices.why: Right. A test whose answers are all `yes` measures whether the model says `yes`, which is something other than the skill it names.

choices.text: Could the questions have been in the training data?
choices.why: That is contamination, a separate problem: memory instead of ability. Here the answers alone give the score away.

choices.text: Is this one run, or many?
choices.why: That question is about demos chosen from many runs. Repeating this test would repeat the same flaw.

choices.text: Who measured it, and can it be repeated?
choices.why: Anybody repeating it would get the same misleading score, because the flaw is in the questions themselves.

prompt: In the ten samples for `question : when does the café open ? answer :`, how many replies began with `yes`?
Which pair of words does lesson 10 apply to a large language model?

choices.text: General, since it covers so many different tasks
choices.why: That breadth comes from one narrow mechanism. General is the word in AGI, which names a goal.

choices.text: Narrow, and not generative, since it only predicts
choices.why: Predicting the next token, over and over, produces new content. That is what generative means.

choices.text: Generative and general, since it does most intellectual tasks
choices.why: That is the description of AGI, a goal with no agreed definition and no agreed test.

choices.text: Generative, and in a real sense narrow
choices.why: Right. It produces new text, and it does one thing, predicting the next token, which covers many tasks written as text.

prompt: For the public holidays question, the top passage was right and the Sunday hours were not retrieved. Where does lesson 11 put the fix?

choices.text: In the grounded prompt's instruction, made stricter
choices.why: The model would follow it faithfully from passages that do not hold the hours. No wording supplies a line that was not retrieved.

choices.text: In a larger model, which would know the Sunday hours
choices.why: No model was trained on this handbook. What is not in the prompt is not known.

choices.text: In how the handbook is cut into passages
choices.why: Right. A cut that separates a rule from the detail it points to is a chunking problem, and the fix is in how the documents are cut.

choices.text: In asking for more passages, so the model sees all of it
choices.why: The missing line shares no word with the question, so it scores zero however many passages are kept.

prompt: One question's top passage scored 8.71 and another question's scored 2.94. What can you conclude?

choices.text: The first match is about three times as good as the second
choices.why: That reads the scores as a scale shared by every question. They only order passages for one query.

choices.text: Nothing about which match is better: scores rank passages for one question
choices.why: Right. The scores are not percentages and have no fixed top, so they mean nothing across questions.

choices.text: The second passage is irrelevant, since it scored under 3
choices.why: There is no score that means not relevant; 2.94 was the exact answer to the Sunday question.

choices.text: The first answer is 87.1% likely to be right
choices.why: BM25 scores are not percentages or probabilities of being right.

prompt: Which of these failures happen before the model writes a word? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Three passages that each share one word, for the cold coffee
choices.why: Yes. The top three are returned whatever they are.

choices.text: A grounded answer with one sentence that cites no source
choices.why: That one is the model's: it went beyond the sources it was given.

choices.text: `wireless internet` finding none of `wifi.md`
choices.why: Yes. The search found nothing, and the model was never shown the answer.

choices.text: The holiday rule retrieved without the Sunday hours
choices.why: Yes. The cut separated the rule from its detail before any model ran.

prompt: The formula `retrieve` uses to score each passage against a question is called ___.
Match each criterion for choosing a model to the question it asks.

pairs.right: How many of your own test cases does it get right?
Does your longest real input fit, with room for the reply?
How long can your user wait for a reply?
When will this exact model be retired?

right_distractors: Which model tops the public comparison table?

prompt: Add up `tok count handbook/*.md` for each encoding. How many more tokens does `cl100k_base` make of the six files than `o200k_base`?
You read a model maker's data terms and they suit you. You will call the same model through a cloud platform that resells it. What does lesson 12 say?

choices.text: Nothing more to check, since the model and its terms are the same
choices.why: The model may be the same. Where you call it from is a decision of its own, with its own terms.

choices.text: Run the weights yourself, since resold models carry no data terms
choices.why: A resold model carries the platform's terms. Running weights yourself is a separate arrangement, and only for open weights.

choices.text: Read the platform's terms too: each place sets its own
choices.why: Right. The same model sold in two places comes with prices, limits, regions and data terms set by each.

choices.text: Check a recent blog post comparing the two platforms' policies
choices.why: Lesson 12 says never to answer these from a blog post: terms change and differ between plans.

prompt: At temperature 1, `toylm` gives `seven` 75% and `eight` 25% after `opens at`. Halving the temperature squares the ratio between two words. What share does `seven` get at temperature 0.5, in percent?
A tool that suggests names for a new café drink runs at temperature 0, and gives the same name every time it is asked. What does lesson 13 suggest?

choices.text: A higher temperature, since you want different candidates on each run
choices.why: Right. Brainstorming has many good answers, and you will throw most candidates away.

choices.text: Keep 0, since it gives the most likely and so the best name
choices.why: The most likely name is not the best one for a task with many good answers. At 0 the others never appear.

choices.text: Keep 0 and change the seed between requests
choices.why: At temperature 0 there is no draw, so the seed has nothing to decide.

choices.text: Raise it to the top of the range, to get the most creative names
choices.why: Change it one step at a time while you watch the output: at the top, nonsense arrives in the same batch.

prompt: Taking the word with the highest score every time, with no draw, is called ___ decoding.
`toylm next "the"` gave `coffee` 29.9%, `café` 18.2%, `bread` 15.6%, `cat` 11.7% and four more below. How many words would `--top-p 0.5` keep there?
Top-p is also called ___ sampling, after the name of the set of words it keeps.
After `at seven`, `toylm` gives the full stop 100%. What does `--top-k 2` keep there?

choices.text: The full stop and the next best word in the vocabulary
choices.why: Only words the model scored can be kept, and it scored one.

choices.text: The full stop alone, since there is one candidate
choices.why: Right. k is the most words kept, and here there is only one to keep.

choices.text: Nothing, since top-k needs at least two candidates
choices.why: Top-k keeps up to k words; fewer candidates simply means fewer kept.

choices.text: Two copies of the full stop, at 50% each
choices.why: There is one word with all of the share, and renormalising leaves it at 100%.

prompt: `request.txt` is 79 input tokens. At the illustrative 2 per million input and 8 per million output, with a limit of 200 output tokens, what is the most 10,000 requests can cost?
A model that reasons before it answers returns a short visible reply with finish reason `length`. Which caution from lesson 15 applies?

choices.text: Some APIs count reasoning tokens against the limit; read the current reference
choices.why: Right. What the parameter counts has changed on some APIs, so the limit might have run out before the visible answer began.

choices.text: The visible reply was short, so the finish reason is a reporting error
choices.why: `length` means the loop was stopped from outside. Treat it as a cut, not as a mistake in the report.

choices.text: A short reply proves the instruction worked, and the reason can be ignored
choices.why: The finish reason is how you find out which of the two happened. A cut answer rarely looks cut.

choices.text: The limit only counts visible text, so the model ended early by choice
choices.why: Choosing to end is `end`. `length` says a limit was reached, whatever it was counting.

prompt: Why are output tokens priced higher than input tokens on most price lists, by lesson 15?

choices.text: Output tokens are longer pieces of text than the input ones
choices.why: A token is the same kind of piece either way; the tokenizer does not change for the reply.

choices.text: Providers charge more for what they write to discourage long replies
choices.why: Lesson 15 gives a reason in the machinery: writing is a step per token, reading is one pass.

choices.text: Output must be checked for safety, and that check is billed per token
choices.why: No such check is part of lesson 15's reason. It is the step per token.

choices.text: Each output token takes a full step of the model; the prompt is one pass
choices.why: Right. The prompt is processed in one pass, and every written token is another step of the loop.

prompt: A plain-text prompt holds eight examples, each a `Message:` line and a `Category:` line, and ends on an open `Category:`. The model writes the category, then a new `Message:` of its own. Which stop fits?

choices.text: `Category:`, since the answer you want follows it
choices.why: It would fire only after an invented message had already been written, one label too late.

choices.text: `e`, the shortest string that ends the reply quickly
choices.why: A short stop fires inside words: `hours` would survive, and `refunds` would come back as `r`.

choices.text: `Message:`, the label that starts the next example
choices.why: Right. It marks the end of the unit you want and does not occur inside a category.

choices.text: No stop: list-of-messages chat APIs end the turn themselves
choices.why: This is plain text with your own markers, which is exactly where stops matter most.

prompt: What does a stop sequence do that lesson 15's token limit does not?

choices.text: It makes the model aware that it should write a single answer
choices.why: The model never learns of the stop. The loop checks the text.

choices.text: It ends the reply at a piece of text that marks the end of the unit
choices.why: Right. A limit cuts at a count, wherever it falls; a stop cuts where a chosen marker appears.

choices.text: It keeps the marker in the output, so the program can find the end
choices.why: The stop text is left out, so a program that needs the marker adds it back.

choices.text: It improves the answer, since the model stops before it can go wrong
choices.why: A stop decides where an answer ends and does nothing for whether it is right.

prompt: A reply lists prices such as `R$ 27.90`, one per line, and somebody sets `.` as a stop so the list ends at the first full stop. What happens?

choices.text: The list is kept whole, since a price is not the end of a sentence
choices.why: The stop is matched as text, not understood. A full stop inside a number is still a full stop.

choices.text: The first price is cut at its decimal point: `R$ 27`
choices.why: Right. A stop fires on the text wherever it appears, and the price contains one.

choices.text: The model learns to write prices with a comma instead
choices.why: The model never learns of the stop; the loop checks the text and cuts it.

choices.text: The reply reports `length`, so the cut is easy to spot
choices.why: A stop reports `stop`, which looks like a normal ending. That is why it is harder to notice.

prompt: In the `the cat` loop, `and` leads `on` by about 0.41. What is the smallest presence penalty, to one decimal place, that breaks the loop the first time `cat sleeps` comes round again?
You want the text pushed towards words it has not used at all, closer to "change the subject" than to "stop grinding on". Which control does lesson 17 point to?

choices.text: The frequency penalty
choices.why: That one leans harder the more a word repeats, which suits loops and lists that grind on.

choices.text: A higher temperature
choices.why: Temperature flattens every score alike; it does not know which words were used.

choices.text: A top-p of 0.8
choices.why: Top-p cuts the unlikely tail, which is the opposite of reaching for unused words.

choices.text: The presence penalty
choices.why: Right. A flat charge for any word already used pushes the text towards new words.

prompt: The prompt is `the cat`. Before `toylm` has written anything, how much does `--presence-penalty 1` subtract from the score of `cat`?

choices.text: 1, since `cat` appears once in the text so far
choices.why: In `toylm` the prompt is not counted. Some APIs do count it, and their reference says so.

choices.text: 1 for each time `cat` appears in the training corpus
choices.why: Penalties look at this output only, never at the training file.

choices.text: Nothing: `toylm` counts the words it wrote, not the prompt
choices.why: Right. The penalty is charged on words already in the output, and the output is still empty.

choices.text: 2, once for `the` and once for `cat`
choices.why: A penalty applies to the word that was used, and nothing was written yet.

prompt: A reply to the review prompt parses cleanly and reads `"staff_praised": "yes"`. What does lesson 18 say is wrong?

choices.text: Nothing, since it parsed and the meaning is clear
choices.why: Clear to a person. Code that tests `staff_praised` for true gets a string, and the string `"no"` is not false either.

choices.text: The parser should have refused it at the first quote
choices.why: `"yes"` is a perfectly good JSON string. The parser has no idea the field was meant to be a boolean.

choices.text: A boolean came back as a word, and parsing does not check types
choices.why: Right. A program needs `true` as a boolean, and a parser only says whether the text is JSON. Lesson 19's schema checks the type.

choices.text: The field name is wrong, and should have been `praised`
choices.why: The name matches the one the prompt gave. The value's type is the problem.

prompt: Python's `csv` reader read the unquoted `replies/menu.csv`, header included. On how many lines did the field count differ from the header's?
Which of these does a JSON parser refuse the moment the reply arrives? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Single quotes around the field names
choices.why: Yes. JSON needs double quotes.

choices.text: A comma after the last field
choices.why: Yes. JSON refuses the trailing comma.

choices.text: A field called `mood` where the prompt said `sentiment`
choices.why: It parses: the parser does not know which names the prompt asked for.

choices.text: A sentence of introduction before the object
choices.why: Yes. JSON has to start with a value, and a letter is not one.

prompt: A reply holds two JSON objects, one after the other, with a sentence between them. What does lesson 19 say `repair` does with it?

choices.text: Step 2 keeps the first object and drops the second
choices.why: Step 2 takes the text from the first `{` to the last `}`, which here holds both objects and the sentence between them.

choices.text: Step 3 merges the two objects and checks the result against the schema
choices.why: Nothing merges objects. Step 3 only checks one object that has already parsed.

choices.text: It sends the follow-up message at once, without trying the cut
choices.why: The cheap steps come first. The follow-up message is for a reply that parsed and failed the schema.

choices.text: Step 2 cuts out text that does not parse, and it says `still not JSON`
choices.why: Right. First `{` to last `}` spans both objects and the sentence, and `repair` reports that rather than guessing further.

prompt: The sketch of the repair loop sets `MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3`. How many retries does that allow after the first reply?
In `schema.json`, the line `"additionalProperties": ___` is what refuses a field the schema never named, such as `mood`.
`validate` printed `(top level): 'summary' is a required property`. What does `(top level)` say?

choices.text: The problem is the most serious of the ones it found
choices.why: The path says where a problem is, not how much it matters.

choices.text: The problem is with the object itself, not with one field inside it
choices.why: Right. A missing required field or an extra one is a fact about the whole object, so its path is the top level.

choices.text: The problem was found on the first line of the file
choices.why: The validator reports paths into the object, not lines and columns; that was the parser in lesson 18.

choices.text: The `summary` field is at the top of the reply but empty
choices.why: The field is absent, and an absent field has no position in the reply.

prompt: Put the checks a reply meant for a program goes through in lesson 19's order, cheapest first, ending with the one that is not a program.
items: Check it against the café's rules
Check that it is true to its input

prompt: On the same eight test messages, how many more did the strong prompt's replies get right than the weak prompt's?
A team's test set holds twenty messages, all as plain as `r1` and `r3`. Two very different prompts both score 20 of 20. What does the result tell them?

choices.text: Both prompts are ready to ship, since neither made a mistake
choices.why: They made no mistake on easy inputs. Sarcasm, questions and other languages were never asked.

choices.text: The longer prompt is better, since it scored the same with more detail
choices.why: Equal scores on easy cases cannot separate the two, let alone favour one.

choices.text: The test set is too large, and eight messages would have been enough
choices.why: Size is not the problem: twenty easy messages and eight easy messages both measure nothing hard.

choices.text: Little: a set with no hard cases scores every prompt well
choices.why: Right. Each line of a test set should be there for a reason, and the reasons are the hard cases: mixed, sarcastic, a question, another language.

prompt: The labeller files `Why was my soup cold again?` as `not_a_review`. The café counts it as a complaint. Following lesson 20, what do you do?

choices.text: Nothing: it is a question, and the prompt says questions are `not_a_review`
choices.why: The café's decision is that this one is a complaint. The prompt has to carry that decision, because the model cannot guess it.

choices.text: Replace the four labels with two, so the model has fewer ways to be wrong
choices.why: The café needs four labels. Fewer labels hides the case instead of deciding it.

choices.text: Add it to the test set as `negative`, and name the case in the prompt
choices.why: Right. Every disagreement is a sentence the prompt needs, and a real message labelled wrong goes into the test set with its right label.

choices.text: Raise the temperature, so the model reads the message more carefully
choices.why: Temperature changes how a word is drawn. It does not tell the model where the café draws this line.

prompt: `tok count` gave `prompt-zero.txt` and `prompt-few.txt`. How many tokens did the four examples add to every request?
A summarising prompt shows three solved cases, and in each the summary is one sentence beginning `The customer`. Nothing in the instructions mentions either. What should you expect back?

choices.text: Whatever length and opening the instructions allow, since they did not ask for these
choices.why: The examples are a specification too, and they say one sentence and that opening.

choices.text: Replies shaped like the examples, down to their first two words
choices.why: Right. Examples teach everything they have in common, whether you meant them to or not.

choices.text: A mix of openings, since three examples are too few to form a pattern
choices.why: One example is already enough to look like a pattern; three that agree are a strong one.

choices.text: Longer summaries, since the model will try to add what the examples left out
choices.why: The model continues the pattern in front of it. Nothing in the pattern says longer.

prompt: Match each rule for choosing examples to what it prevents.

pairs.right: One label looking like the default
Examples that teach nothing the description had not
The last example's label leaking into the answer

pairs.left: Keep them out of the test set
pairs.right: A score that measures memory

right_distractors: A prompt too long to send

prompt: To save tokens, an application sends the system message only with the first request of each conversation. What happens from the second request on?

choices.text: Nothing changes, since the model remembers the system message
choices.why: There is no memory between requests. The system message holds only because it is sent every time.

choices.text: The rules still hold, because precedence is enforced by the API
choices.why: Precedence is trained, not enforced, and it needs the text to be there in the first place.

choices.text: The model asks the application to send the rules again
choices.why: It has no way to know rules existed. It continues whatever text it is given.

choices.text: The model works with no standing instructions at all
choices.why: Right. The model keeps nothing between requests, so a system message left out of a request does not exist for it.

prompt: `prompts/system-v3.txt` is 149 tokens and goes with every message. How many input tokens does it account for over 10,000 customer messages?
A security review asks what an attacker would learn if the café assistant's system prompt were revealed in full. If lesson 22 was followed, what is the answer?

choices.text: The staff Wi-Fi password, which the model was told never to reveal
choices.why: That is what lesson 22 says never to put there: what the model must not tell, it must not be given.

choices.text: The customer records sent with each question
choices.why: Customer data has no place in a system prompt, and the café's has none.

choices.text: Nothing that does harm: it was written as if it would be published
choices.why: Right. No passwords, no keys, no customer data, no notes on which rules are really enforced.

choices.text: Nothing at all, since a system prompt cannot be revealed
choices.why: It can: it is text in the model's context, and lesson 7 shows how it comes back out.

prompt: Lesson 23 says the role that changes a reply most is often not the model's but the ___'s: who the reply is for.
Which of these lines sets the reader's role rather than the model's?

choices.text: Explain to a new barista, on their first day, why we ask about allergies
choices.why: Right. It names who the reply is for, which sets the register, the vocabulary and the angle at once.

choices.text: You are a patient teacher who explains things to people slowly
choices.why: That casts the model, not the reader. Who the explanation is for is still open.

choices.text: You are the assistant at Café Aurora's counter: warm, brief, plain
choices.why: That is the model's role, a voice for every reply.

choices.text: You are a world-class food allergy specialist
choices.why: That is a role for the model, and one that adds tone and no knowledge.

prompt: The café's website assistant answers correctly in a stiff, formal voice, and the café wants it warm and brief. What is the cheapest fix, by lesson 23?

choices.text: Fine-tuning on a few hundred warm, brief replies
choices.why: That is the dearest rung of lesson 9's ladder, for something one line of prompt does.

choices.text: A longer handbook, so the assistant has more to say
choices.why: More facts change what it knows, not how it sounds, and brief is the opposite of more.

choices.text: Twenty examples of warm replies on every request
choices.why: Examples are paid for on every request, and a role line does the same job for a few tokens.

choices.text: One role line in the system message, giving the voice
choices.why: Right. A role is one line that changes the register of every reply after it, which is the job here.

prompt: `tok count` gave 40 tokens for `bare.txt` and 216 for `with-context.txt`. How many times the bare prompt is the one with context? Give one decimal place.
The café's assistant carries the whole handbook in its system prompt. Is that system prompting or contextual prompting, by lesson 24?

choices.text: System prompting only, since anything in the system message is an instruction
choices.why: The system message holds instructions, and it can also hold facts. Lesson 24 says the facts live in either place.

choices.text: Contextual only, since a system prompt holds no facts
choices.why: A system prompt may carry the handbook. Lesson 24 says the facts live in either place.

choices.text: Both: the facts are context wherever they sit
choices.why: Right. What makes it contextual is the question asked while writing: what does the model need to know that it cannot know otherwise?

choices.text: Neither: it is retrieval, since the handbook is a document
choices.why: Retrieval chooses passages by program for each request. Pasting the whole handbook once in the system prompt is not that.

prompt: The same R$ 140 refund now needs a note for the shift manager to approve, not an e-mail to the customer. Which kind of context changes first?

choices.text: The data
choices.why: The refunds page and the customer's message are the same material. The reader is what moved.

choices.text: Who the answer is for
choices.why: Right. A note for the shift manager differs in tone and shape from a reply to a customer about the same refund.

choices.text: Nothing, since the facts of the refund are the same
choices.why: The facts are, and the reader is not. Who the answer is for decides tone and shape.

choices.text: The model, since a manager's note is a different task
choices.why: The same model can write both. The prompt has to say who the note is for.

prompt: `direct.txt` is 116 tokens; the step-back version sends `step1.txt` (122) and then `step2.txt` (301). How many more input tokens does the step-back version send than the direct one?
At the counter: "A customer's wrong dish cost R$ 120. Can I refund it on the spot?" Which is a step-back question for it, in lesson 25's sense?

choices.text: Which handbook rules decide when a refund needs someone's approval?
choices.why: Right. It asks for the rules the case is an instance of, including the exception above R$ 100 that the wording hides.

choices.text: Exactly which dish did the customer order, and what was wrong with it?
choices.why: That goes further into the specifics, the opposite direction from a step back.

choices.text: Can I refund it on the spot? Answer yes or no, then explain.
choices.why: That is the original question again, with a format added.

choices.text: Is R$ 120 a large amount for a single dish at a café?
choices.why: That asks for an opinion about the price, not for the rule that decides the case.

prompt: Which of these questions have the shape lesson 25 says a step back helps? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: An exception hidden behind a more obvious rule
choices.why: Yes, the holiday toastie's shape: the wording points at the wrong rule.

choices.text: A question from a field with laws, such as physics
choices.why: Yes. Naming the law is most of the work, as with the gas question.

choices.text: One moment in a longer history, such as a career
choices.why: Yes. The whole history in the prompt is what the date is read against.

choices.text: The name of the guest Wi-Fi network
choices.why: There is no principle behind it: the answer is one line of the handbook.

prompt: Work it out step by step, as lesson 26 asks of the model. A customer orders 4 espressos at R$ 9 each and 1 cinnamon bun at R$ 11. Their loyalty card already has 8 stamps, and the tenth coffee is free. How many reais do they pay?
A program needs both the chain and an answer it can parse without fail. Beyond a fixed `Answer:` line, what does lesson 26 point to?

choices.text: The last number in the reply, which is where the answer usually sits
choices.why: Picking a number out of the text is the guess the fixed marker was there to avoid; the chain is full of numbers.

choices.text: A structured format, with the reasoning and the answer in separate fields
choices.why: Right. Lesson 18's formats put the reasoning in one field and the answer in another, and a parser checks both.

choices.text: A second request asking the model to repeat only its answer
choices.why: That doubles the calls and gives another reply to parse, with the same problem.

choices.text: A higher output limit, so the answer line is never cut off
choices.why: A limit set too low can cut the chain before `Answer:`, but raising it does not make the answer easier to read out.

prompt: Which of these would gain from asking for the steps first, by lesson 26? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The price of one flat white, read off the menu
choices.why: A one-step question has no intermediate result, and gains nothing.

choices.text: A bill over several items, with a discount rule
choices.why: Yes: a rule applied before a sum needs an intermediate result.

choices.text: Two handbook facts that have to be combined
choices.why: Yes. The first fact, written down, is what the second step is conditioned on.

choices.text: A sum of six prices with a total at the end
choices.why: Yes. Arithmetic over several items has intermediate results to write.

prompt: The seven café chains came to 1,539 output tokens. A vote of twenty-one samples, with chains of the same average length, would cost how many output tokens?
On the holiday question, the vote came out `yes` in four of the four samples that wrote an answer line, and the handbook says `no`. What does lesson 27 propose?

choices.text: Draw twenty samples instead of five, so the right answer can catch up
choices.why: More samples of the same prompt repeat the same pull, and the wrong majority would most likely grow firmer.

choices.text: Sample at temperature 0, so every chain follows the most careful path
choices.why: At temperature 0 every sample is a copy, and a vote among copies is no vote.

choices.text: Keep the fifth sample's conclusion, since its chain reasons through the rule
choices.why: Choosing by how a chain reads is what a vote was meant to replace. The prompt is where the pull starts.

choices.text: Step back to the rules first, then vote among chains that start from them
choices.why: Right. The wrong chains share one pull, the word Wednesday, and the fix is in the prompt, before the samples are drawn.

prompt: Match each technique to what happens to a dead end, by lesson 28's comparison table.

pairs.right: It is followed to the end
It is outvoted, if it is rare
It is dropped when it is judged

right_distractors: It is repaired by the loop and retried

prompt: At level 2 of `tot 4 9 10 13` with the default breadth, how many of the proposed states were repeats of a state already proposed?
On some problem, most attempts take the same tempting first step, and it leads to a dead end that can be recognised once you are there. Which technique handles that best, by lesson 28's table?

choices.text: Self-consistency, which outvotes the dead end
choices.why: A vote outvotes a dead end only if it is rare. When most samples take it, the wrong answer wins.

choices.text: Tree of thoughts, which drops the step when it is judged
choices.why: Right. A tree judges partial states at every step, so a dead end is cut before anything more is spent on it.

choices.text: Chain of thought, which writes the steps out one by one
choices.why: A single chain follows its first step to the end, with no way back.

choices.text: Any of the three, since each one compares paths at every step
choices.why: Only the tree compares at every step. A chain never compares, and a vote compares only final answers.

prompt: Put the three techniques in order of model calls per answer, fewest first.
Match each kind of line in a ReAct trace to what it holds.

pairs.right: What is known so far, and what is needed next
One tool, and what to give it
What the tool returned, word for word
The reply, once nothing more is needed

right_distractors: The model's guess at what the tool will return

prompt: A stock tool returns `0` whenever its database is down, instead of an error. What does lesson 29 say that does to a ReAct run?

choices.text: Nothing, since the model will notice the database is down
choices.why: Nothing in `0` says the database is down. The model reasons from what the Observation says.

choices.text: The loop stops the run, since `0` is not a valid Observation
choices.why: The loop checks the shape of turns, not whether a tool's reply is true. `0` is a perfectly shaped reply.

choices.text: The run ends at the step limit, since the model keeps retrying
choices.why: With `0` there is nothing to retry: the model has been told there is no stock and moves on.

choices.text: It hands the model a wrong fact to reason from
choices.why: Right. A clear error comes back as an Observation the next turn acts on; a silent `0` reads as a true answer.

prompt: Both lesson 30's prompt tuning and lesson 31's automatic prompt engineering find a prompt instead of writing one. What separates them?

choices.text: One learns vectors against the weights; the other scores written prompts
choices.why: Right. Prompt tuning needs the weights and a gradient. APE needs only a way to send text and a set of labelled examples.

choices.text: Prompt tuning changes the weights; APE leaves them as they are
choices.why: Neither changes the weights. In prompt tuning they are frozen and only the soft prompt's numbers move.

choices.text: APE needs the weights, and prompt tuning works through any API
choices.why: The other way round: through an API there is nowhere to put a vector, while APE sends ordinary text.

choices.text: Only APE produces something a model can be given
choices.why: Both produce something a model can be given. Only APE's result can also be read by a person.

prompt: In lesson 30's table, which of the three is paid for as extra tokens of text sent with every request?

choices.text: The written prompt
choices.why: Right. Its cost is the tokens of the prompt, on every request, as lesson 3 counted.

choices.text: Prompt tuning
choices.why: Its cost is a training run, then almost nothing per request: the vectors are not text.

choices.text: Fine-tuning
choices.why: It costs a training run and often a higher price per request, and it adds no prompt text.

choices.text: None of them, since a model is priced per answer
choices.why: Models are priced per token, and the written prompt's tokens go with every request.

prompt: In prompt tuning, the soft prompt's numbers are trained while the model's own weights stay ___.
`the {x} is` scored 4/4 on `tests.tsv`. What was its score on `held.tsv`, as a percentage rounded to the nearest whole number?
Lesson 21 warned that a prompt whose examples are the test set's own messages scores well for the wrong reason. Which idea in lesson 31 is the same warning?

choices.text: The proposer's job is variety and the scorer's is judgement
choices.why: That splits the work between two steps. It says nothing about which examples may measure the result.

choices.text: Examples used to choose cannot measure the choice honestly
choices.why: Right. The winner's 4/4 used `tests.tsv` up, and a held-out set measures honestly once per decision.

choices.text: Exact match can score a correct reply as wrong
choices.why: That is a fault in the metric, and it applies whatever examples are used.

choices.text: A person approves what goes into production
choices.why: That catches what a score cannot, such as a harmful assumption. It is a different safeguard.

prompt: Put an honest run of automatic prompt engineering in order.
items: A model proposes candidate prompts from a few examples
Each candidate is scored on the labelled examples
The winner is scored once on the held-out set
A person reads the winner before it goes into production
